content: Cicuta, commonly known as Water Hemlock or Cowbane, is a small genus comprising four species of highly toxic flowering plants belonging to the Apiaceae family. These plants are native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with a primary distribution in North America. They are perennial herbaceous plants that can grow up to 2 meters in height. These species typically thrive in wet meadows, along streambanks, and in other marshy or waterlogged areas. Despite their superficial resemblance to Poison Hemlock (genus Conium), which is also a member of the Apiaceae family, Cicuta species are distinct. The stems of Cicuta plants are smooth, branching, and swollen at the base. They may exhibit purple stripes or mottling (as seen in Cicuta maculata) and are hollow except for partitions located at the junctions of the leaves and stems. The leaves are arranged alternately, are tripinnate, and have coarse, toothed edges, differing from the fern-like, lacy leaves characteristic of many other Apiaceae members. The flowers are small, white, and grouped in umbrella-shaped clusters, a hallmark of this plant family. When the stems or roots are cut, they exude an oily, yellow liquid with a strong, unpleasant odor reminiscent of parsnips, carrots, or mice. Cicuta is extremely toxic and is sometimes mistaken for parsnips due to its clusters of white, tuberous roots. This misidentification can be fatal, as Cicuta is considered one of the most poisonous plants in North America. Ingestion of any part of the plant can result in death, often preceded by violent and painful convulsions. While humans have succumbed to Cicuta poisoning over the centuries, livestock are particularly vulnerable, leading to the plant's common name Cowbane. Death in livestock can occur within as little as 15 minutes after ingestion. The primary toxic compound in Cicuta is cicutoxin, an unsaturated aliphatic alcohol that is most concentrated in the roots. In humans, symptoms of poisoning typically manifest within 30 to 60 minutes of consumption and include nausea, vomiting, and tremors. These initial symptoms are followed by severe abdominal cramps, projectile vomiting, and convulsions. In some cases, long-term effects such as retrograde amnesia have been reported. The four recognized species of Cicuta are as follows: Cicuta bulbifera (Bulblet-bearing Water Hemlock): Found in northern North America. Cicuta douglasii (Western Water Hemlock): Found in western North America. Cicuta maculata (Spotted Water Hemlock): Widespread across North America. Cicuta virosa (Cowbane or Northern Water Hemlock): Found in northern Europe, Asia, and Alaska.
